News.title: Concrete mixer bursts into flames on Scottish residential street
News.content:
A concrete mixer burst into flames on a residential street in Scotland this afternoon.

The blaze erupted around 3.30pm on Monday, March 30 when emergency services were called to Admiralty Road in Rosyth, Fife.

According to Daily Record, Police Scotland and Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, rushed to the scene. Two appliances and a hose reel jet were deployed in to calm the blaze, images from the incident show large orange flames engulf the Beatson's truck.

The company is reportedly a ready mix concrete supplier based in Alloa, Clackmannanshire. A firefighter can be seen spraying water on the vehicle, which is parked up on the roadside.

Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as your Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

Another truck can be seen parked behind it. Fire crews confirmed the fire was eventually brought under control and extinguished, with personnel able to leave the scene an hour later.

No one was injured but the cause of the blaze is unclear.

Image: Fife Jammer Locations) Fife Jammer Locations)

Police Scotland said they attended only to assist with road closures and there was nothing suspicious to report. The road has since reopened.

A Scottish Fire and Rescue Service spokesperson said: "We got a call at 3.330pm about a vehicle fire on Admiralty Road, Rosyth on Monday, March 30. We mobilised two appliances and crews put the fire out with one hose reel jet.

"Crews left the scene at 4.34pm. There were no casualties."

A Police Scotland spokesperson added: "Officers attended the scene of a vehicle fire on Admiralty Road, Rosyth to assist with road closures. The road has since reopened.

"The fire was not suspicious and there were no injuries."

News.title: Teenager admits staggering £140k shoplifting spree from major high street stores
News.content:
Teenager admits staggering £140k shoplifting spree from major high street stores

The boy - aged just 17 - was said to be "shocked" after his grandfather told him he could be jailed for FIFTEEN counts of theft from Boots and Holland and Barrett during a two-year campaign

View 3 Images Highbury Magistrates' Court was told the youngster took cosmetic products from the shelves in dozens of raids (Image: Alamy Stock Photo)

A teenage boy has admitted carrying out a brazen shoplifting spree totalling nearly £140,000 at Boots and Holland and Barrett.

The 17-year-old took cosmetic products from the shelves in dozens of raids on the London branches of the high street giants over the last two years, magistrates at Highbury Corner Youth Court heard.

The teenager, who cannot be named because of his age, pleaded guilty to 15 counts of theft — which included 11 counts where he took goods valued at £59,280.07 from Boots.

He had been charged with 56 counts of shoplifting from Boots, and the court was told the other 45 offences would be taken into consideration. On Monday, he also pleaded guilty to another four thefts at Holland and Barrett, where goods worth more than £2,415 were taken.

View 3 Images The court was told he stole goods valued at £137,342.52 from Boots between April 2024 and December 2025 (Image: PA)

He stole goods valued at £137,342.52 from Boots between April 2024 and December 2025, and a haul worth more than £2,415 from Holland and Barrett from October 2025 to this January, the court was told.

The boy has been "shocked" by a warning from his grandfather that he could end up in prison if he does not turn his life around, the court heard.

Asked by the magistrates about the reasons behind his prolific offending, the boy replied: "Sometimes I just get distracted and led by other people, and stuff like that. I do not want to be like that anymore. I just want to be with my granddad."

The boy, who towered over his mother who sat beside him in court, lowered his head into his hands as his charges were being read. His mother said: "He is easily influenced. We did not know anything about this.

View 3 Images He also stole a haul worth more than £2,415 from Holland and Barrett between October 2025 to this January (Image: Getty Images)

"We have spoken to him about the consequences of it — prison — and he does not want to go down that road. My dad is showing him and hoping he will make a change." Chair of the magistrates' bench Jennifer Shewry said the grandfather has "shocked him", and the mother replied "yes".

Prosecutor Edward Kalber called for the case to be deal with at crown court "to give maximum latitude for the sentencing decision". Describing this case as having "unique circumstances and unique events", the prosecutor said: "If he was an adult I would say that this should go straight to the crown court.

"The amount of money taken is significant and he is targeting businesses. The impact on the businesses is high." He added: "He has repeatedly targeted businesses, some of these offences are repeated at the same venue."

He targeted Boots shops in Westminster, Lambeth, Camden and Kensington and Chelsea — along with Holland and Barrett stores in Hammersmith and Fulham and Camden. His guilty pleas included his highest value theft, where he stole £9,316.05 worth of goods from a Boots in Kensington and Chelsea on October 2, 2024.

He was identified through CCTV stealing items in the company of another youth. No further details were given about the other youth. Sentencing was adjourned to May 7 and the teenager was freed on bail with a condition that he does not go to any Boots or Holland and Barrett store in England and Wales, unless he is accompanied by a family member.

Article continues below

Mrs Shewry told him "we do not get cases like this very often", and further information may be needed for his sentencing. She also warned him: "You need to stay out of trouble. This would only get worse. If you were to breach those conditions, you will end up in court. "

News.title: Stephen Lawrence's dad's fury at new blow to legacy of son's racist murder
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Stephen Lawrence's dad's fury at new blow to legacy of son's racist murder

Neville Lawrence fears lives will be lost if police stop recording certain hate crime incidents 27 years after a landmark report into his son's racist murder called for them to do so

Stephen Lawrence’s father warns hate rule change ‘could spark violence’

Stephen Lawrence's father has spoken of his distress at plans to drop a key recommendation of the landmark report into his son's racist murder.

‌



Neville Lawrence said he had not been consulted over the decision by police chiefs to call for the scrapping of non-crime hate incidents. NCHIs are defined as being motivated by hostility or prejudice towards people with certain characteristics, such as race or gender, but which do not meet the bar for a criminal offence.

‌



Sir William Macpherson’s 1999 report into Stephen’s murder recommended that the term “racist incident” should explicitly include both crimes and non-crimes.

‌



“Both must be reported, recorded and investigated with equal commitment,” Sir William said. But a review by the National Police Chiefs' Council and the College of Policing is soon expected to recommend NCHIs be scrapped.

View 6 Images Stephen Lawrence was murdered in 1993 (Image: PA)

Mr Lawrence, 84, said he fears it could result in lives being lost. He told the Daily Mirror: "At least when a racial incident happens the police can go and investigate it. Without that being done a lot of people are going to get really angry and maybe turn to violence.

‌



"They [the police] are the people that make the public feel safe. People are going to take the law into their own hands and somebody might get killed.

"There are supposed to be laws to make sure people can live decent lives. If the police aren't going to record these incidents then who are?

"This is going back on what Lord Macpherson's inquiry did 27 years ago, back to where they used to be. "

‌



Mark Hobrough, formerly the lead officer for hate crime for the NPCC, stood down from the position earlier this month after his advisor Paul Giannasi resigned in protest over the issue. The NPCC said Mr Hobrough left the role for "capacity reasons" because of his "demanding" workload.

View 6 Images Paul Giannasi OBE has stood down over the issue

Supporters of NCHIs argue that the recording of the data is vital for helping the police spot early warning signs that could later escalate into serious crimes.

‌



They cite the case of Fiona Pilkington, who killed herself and her severely disabled daughter Francecca Hardwick in 2007 after 33 recorded incidents of contact between her and police regarding abuse from local youths.

View 6 Images Fiona Pilkington, who killed herself and her severely disabled daughter (Image: PA)

The victim led approach also helps to build much needed trust in the police by showing that all forms of hate will be taken seriously. It can also be a useful tool for informing policy and policing strategy.

‌



Chief Constable Gavin Stephens, chair of the NPCC, said on Monday: “In a world which feels increasingly polarised and divided, it is even more important that victims of hate have the confidence to report to the police. Maintaining public confidence has been a driving force behind all of this work.

“Policing is clear that this new system must recognise vulnerability, ensure hate crimes are properly recorded, and that community tensions and potential precursors to violence and other crimes are identified.

“It is vital that we know this works for our communities and builds public trust and confidence in our service. That’s why this review is just the start of this process and we will now be working with both policing and our communities to work through these changes and ensure the new system is clearly understood, fair and effectively implemented.”

‌



John Azah OBE, a member of the Hate Crime Independent Advisory group, said: "I report the case, it's your job as the police to find out if it's a hate incident or a hate crime.

"Before the Stephen Lawrence inquiry there wasn't a clear definition of what constituted a hate crime. The primary issue that affects us is that if you say you are not going to investigate racist incidents what will happen if Neville is walking down the street and someone spits at him? If you are not able to report that to the police how can it be decided whether it reaches the criminal threshold?"

View 6 Images John Azah has raised concerns about the proposal (Image: itv)

‌



Stephen, 18, was stabbed to death by a gang of up to six youths shouting "what, what n*****" at a bus stop in Eltham, south-east London, on April 22, 1993.

Mr Lawrence and his ex-wife Baroness Doreen Lawrence fought for justice after they were repeatedly failed by the Metropolitan Police who bungled the investigation and spied on their campaign.

View 6 Images Baroness Doreen Lawrence was forced to fight for justice for her son (Image: Rowan Griffiths / Daily Mirror)

‌



It took until 2012 for David Norris, 48, and Gary Dobson, 49, to be convicted of murder. The rest remained free and the investigation was closed in 2020.

Former Met-detective Clive Driscoll, who led the probe into Dobson and Norris, said of the proposed change: "I believe the Lawrence family would be unhappy if Lord Macpherson's recommendations were not followed."

View 6 Images Ex-Met DCI Clive Driscoll (Image: BBC Inside Out West)

Article continues below

College of Policing chair and Conservative Lord, Nick Herbert has previously said focusing only on the most serious incidents would "re-balance the system" for the social media age.

Danny Stone, chief executive of the Antisemitism Policy Trust, wrote in 2022: "Victim-led hate reporting has had significant and important positive impacts for police, and communities, in diagnosing harm, extremism, and failing integration or community-cohesion efforts … We all know that recording rules can be complex, but they should not be a concern to a victim at their time of distress.”

The home secretary will have the final decision on whether to adopt the recommendations. The College of Policing declined to comment.

News.title: King Charles stocks up teddies at Sandringham shop amid shamed Andrew moving in
News.content:
King Charles stocks up teddies at Sandringham shop amid shamed Andrew moving in

Pictures have shown piles of teddy bears on sale inside the King's official gift shop in Sandringham - as his brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, known for a huge cuddly toy collection, moves to his new home on the estate

View 4 Images Piles of teddy bears on sale in the Sandringham shop (Image: Bav Media)

King Charles' official shop at Sandringham has stocked up with piles of teddy bears - amid Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's move to his new permanent home on the estate. Snaps show dozens of cuddly toys for sale in the shop, which is open to visitors to the Norfolk estate.

The bears, which are being sold for £14.99, include one wearing a knitted jumper with the word Sandringham across it and another showing a bear in a crown and a robe. It comes as former prince Andrew, known for his apparent vast collection of cuddly toys, prepares to move into his new permanent home of Marsh Farm on the Sandringham estate.

View 4 Images The £14.99 bears wear a knitted jumper with the word Sandringham across it (Image: Bav Media)

The former Duke of York was booted out of Royal Lodge, a 30-room Windsor mansion, in January following the latest release of the Epstein files.

He set up a temporary home at Wood Farm in Sandringham, where he was arrested on his 66th birthdat last month. But in the coming days, he is expected to move into the nearby five bedroom cottage, Marsh Farm, which has undergone extensive renovations in order to make it habitable for him.

In recent weeks, there have been a number of deliveries at Marsh Farm, with removal workers seen taking boxes labelled 'HRH' into the property. It's unknown if the contents include his collection of teddies, which a former Buckingham Palace maid claimed he would have arranged on his bed in size order.

View 4 Images Some teddies wear a crown and a cape (Image: Bav Media)

Charlotte Briggs, who worked at the Palace in the 90s, once claimed that the toys had to be lined up in size order, and it took staff an entire day to be trained on how to arrange them on his bed.

Meanwhile, new security fences have been erected, with a Sky TV engineer seen installing television and broadband services. Royal sources have confirmed that the King has met the refurbishment costs himself due to his brother’s wrecked finances.

Last week, a mobile home was delivered to Sandringham and installed next to his new home of Marsh Farm. Sources have confirmed the luxury caravan will be used for security staff, paid for by the King, to stay over when needed.

It comes as the King has given an order to his disgraced brother, which has left aides in a race against time to remove any trace of the disgraced ex-royal. The monarch last month brought forward a deadline for Mountbatten-Windsor to clear Royal Lodge of his belongings.

View 4 Images The King with his younger brother, the disgraced former Duke of York (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Royal aides have in the past few days been clearing out the remaining possessions from Royal Lodge, including the staff quarters where Andrew was waited on night and day by royal flunkies.

A number of skips have been loaded and removed from the estate, with removal vans seen coming and going. Staff have also been setting fire to further unwanted belongings of their own.

Article continues below

The King commanded his shamed brother to leave the Windsor home he had lived in for over 20 years, paying a peppercorn rent after signing an initial lease worth £7.5million in 2002. Andrew denies any wrongdoing.

News.title: Top 10 most awkward moments in life leaving Brits embarrassed
News.content:
Top 10 most awkward moments in life leaving Brits embarrassed

A new survey has revealed the top ten most awkward moments that leave Brits feeling uncomfortable

View 2 Images Brits have been left red in the face after texting the wrong person (Image: Getty Images)

According to research, some of the most uncomfortable moments in life include calling someone by the wrong name and falling over in public. Polling suggests that 37% of UK adults frequently experience embarrassing or awkward encounters, with many noting that the nation as a whole is prone to these uncomfortable moments.

‌



A survey of 2,000 adults revealed that having a growling stomach in a quiet room full of people (32%) and accidentally getting into the wrong car (21%) are also considered highly mortifying experiences. Additionally, sending a message to the wrong group chat (31%) was cited as another particularly uncomfortable moment.

‌



View 2 Images Running and missing a bus is considered one of the most embarrassing moments (Image: Getty Images)

‌



For 40% of Gen Z, trying to grab somebody’s attention and being ignored is the most awkward and uncomfortable thing that can happen, with 19% most likely to pretend it never did. But 21% of Millennials consider greeting someone with the wrong handshake the worst of the bunch.

The research was commissioned by Samsung to mark the launch of Galaxy Buds4 Pro, which are designed to adjust to real‑world conditions and everyday situations by automatically adjusting volume and noise-cancelling depending on external factors.

‌



For 48% having earbuds nearby after an awkward moment provides a welcome sense of comfort. Four in ten also revealed they find it easier to get through uncomfortable situations when wearing them.

It emerged women were likely to find tripping up most embarrassing (47%), whereas men put calling someone the wrong name as top of their troubles (45%).

But more than one in five will laugh at themselves when an embarrassing moment occurs. Another 49% will make a self‑deprecating joke and move on, while 12% double down confidently, pretending the faux pas was intentional.

Article continues below

Nearly half (49%) admitted they can let it go when they know it’ll make for a good story later. They also admit these moments can feel worse when in unfamiliar company.

A fifth added that an uncomfortable incident usually sticks with them for only a few minutes, but one in ten claimed it lingers for 'several days'.

THE TOP 10 MOST AWKWARD MOMENTS IN LIFE:

News.title: Do 1 simple thing before moving to keep important documents safe
News.content:
Do 1 simple thing before moving to keep important documents safe

Brit are being urged to take one simple step before moving house to make sure they keep important documents safe

View 2 Images Moving house can be a stressful process and misplacing items can make it even worse (Image: Getty Images)

Chargers, clothes and furniture screws are the most common things people lose in a house move. A poll of 1,000 adults who have moved house in the last five years found 14% ended up shelling out more than £150 to replace lost belongings. Other commonly misplaced items included books (26%) or single socks and shoes (21%). Meanwhile, 52% admitted to breaking an average of four items while moving, costing them £82 each time.

‌



The research was commissioned by the HMRC app which has teamed up with moving firm Pickfords to help customers stay on top of important admin during stressful moments like moving house.

‌



View 2 Images Important documents can easily get lost if not properly stored away (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Sarah McMann, chief digital product owner, for the app said: “Moving home can be stressful, there’s a lot to keep on top of and it’s easy for important documents to get lost along the way.

“We can help ease that pressure by keeping your tax information safe, secure and easy to access.”

The study found important documents are what people are most worried about losing when moving house (59%) – outranking those worried about losing electronics or furniture – with most people worried about losing their passports, birth certificates and driver’s licenses.

‌



Nearly nine in 10 of those polled find moving home stressful, with the physical move being the worst part for 51%, while another 38% dread having to update their new address.

A further 75% say the process of moving feels chaotic and rushed, with 80% saying an app to help track important documents would make the process easier, according to the OnePoll.com figures.

‌



The study found 29% of those who have moved took over three weeks to update their address details with key institutions such as bands, utilities and doctor’s surgeries.

Which may be due to only 63% being confident they could even find their key documents quickly after making a house move.
